title: Automating System Administration
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Automating System Administration and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate automating system administration.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces automating system administration as part of shell scripting and automation. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Write scripts that validate input, handle errors, log clearly, and safely automate repeatable work.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable automation validates inputs, handles expected failures, quotes expansions, writes useful logs, and can be rerun safely.

items.title: User and group reports
items.text: User and group reports: Check the effective identity and policy, prefer the minimum required privileges, and verify both allowed and denied access in a test environment.

items.title: Disk-space monitoring
items.text: Disk-space monitoring: Identify the relevant path or storage layer first, inspect its current state, and make changes only in a disposable lab with a recovery plan.

items.title: Service-health checks
items.text: Service-health checks: Include timestamps and enough context to connect the event to a service or process; choose a threshold that leads to a concrete action.

items.title: Log rotation and cleanup tasks
items.text: Log rotation and cleanup tasks: Include timestamps and enough context to connect the event to a service or process; choose a threshold that leads to a concrete action.

items.title: Software inventory scripts
items.text: Software inventory scripts: Try a small reproducible command with quoted inputs, inspect standard output and error separately, and check the exit status as well as the printed text.

content_blocks.execution_mode: manual-terminal; requires a local Linux environment or disposable VM; no isolated Linux runner is provided by CodeLeaf
content_blocks.code: printf 'inspect -> validate -> change in lab -> verify -> record\n'
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Automating System Administration. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume automating system administration behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: This is an inspection command. Formatting, partitioning, and repair commands can destroy data. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Reliable automation validates inputs, handles expected failures, quotes expansions, writes useful logs, and can be rerun safely. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate automating system administration. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Reliable automation validates inputs, handles expected failures, quotes expansions, writes useful logs, and can be rerun safely.
Use evidence rather than assumptions; make platform differences explicit.
Protect credentials and data, and plan how to reverse state-changing operations.
